snapshots.query: Enact Systems vs Solo for solar proposals
snapshots.answerText:
For residential sales presentations, I’d lean Solo. For an installer-led design-and-proposal workflow, I’d lean Enact. That’s my assessment of their current offerings—not a hands-on benchmark.

Key differences

| Area | Enact Systems | Solo |
|---|---|---|
| Main emphasis | Solar/storage design, financial analysis, and customized proposals. | Interactive sales presentations, live pricing changes, financing, and closing. |
| Proposal workflow | Build the system, model economics, then generate a branded proposal with customized graphs, imagery, and pricing. | Guide the homeowner through an interactive presentation; adjust equipment, pricing, and financing during the appointment. |
| Design support | 3D roof modeling, shading analysis, and battery sizing within the platform. | Self-service design plus an optional concierge team that builds designs and proposals for you. |
| Financing and signing | Loan, lease, and PPA modeling; DocuSign support. | Embedded lender applications and e-signatures within the sales flow. |
| Likely best fit | Teams that want to control design and economics themselves. | Sales organizations prioritizing consistent presentations and reducing proposal-preparation work. |

Feature sources: Enact’s platform, Solo Solar Studio, and Solo’s concierge service.

Pricing

Enact: Lists $279/month billed annually, or $299 month-to-month for two users, with unlimited residential projects/proposals and 10 new commercial projects monthly. Engineering and asset management are separately priced. Enact pricing

Solo: Its current pricing page doesn’t publish dollar amounts. Plans vary by usage, support, and scale; unlimited users and onboarding are included. Get a written quote covering self-service, concierge designs, revisions, and integrations. Solo pricing

My recommendation

Choose Solo if:

Reps present live and need to change pricing or financing immediately.

You want outsourced proposal/design capacity.

Standardizing the sales process across multiple reps matters most.

Choose Enact if:

Your team does its own design and financial modeling.

You handle a mix of residential and commercial projects.

You prefer a published subscription price with unlimited residential proposals.

Don’t decide on proposal appearance alone. Have both vendors model the same three real jobs and compare production estimates, utility assumptions, battery savings, revision speed, and total cost—including staff time. Their marketing doesn’t establish which is more accurate.

Are you selling in Canada or the U.S., and roughly how many proposals per month? Those details could change the recommendation substantially.

snapshots.query: challenges of manual solar quoting for growing businesses
snapshots.answerText:
Challenges of manual solar quoting for growing businesses

Manual quoting—using spreadsheets, separate design tools, and individually assembled proposals—can become a bottleneck as lead volume grows. The main challenges are:

Slower sales turnaround. Gathering customer data, designing systems, calculating prices, and preparing proposals takes staff time. Delays give competitors more opportunity to win the customer, a risk highlighted in Aurora Solar’s industry playbook.

Errors and costly rework. Copying information between tools increases opportunities for mismatched designs, missing details, and outdated proposal versions. Aurora identifies disconnected sales and design workflows as sources of redesigns and change orders. Source

Complex savings calculations. Credible estimates depend on electricity consumption, system size, roof orientation, sunlight, financing, utility rates, and export compensation. Manually maintaining these inputs makes consistent, customer-specific quoting harder. U.S. Department of Energy

Difficulty expanding into new markets. Local permitting and utility requirements vary. Teams must account for those differences rather than reuse assumptions that may underestimate costs or timelines. National Laboratory of the Rockies

Inconsistent pricing and margins. Without shared pricing rules and approval controls, different employees may use different equipment costs, discounts, or installation allowances. The practical risk is winning work that delivers less profit than expected.

Growth tied to headcount. If each quote requires substantial manual effort, more leads mean more staffing—or longer queues. Reliance on a few experienced estimators also creates a capacity bottleneck.

Bottom line: The scaling problem is not just producing quotes faster. It is maintaining accuracy, consistent margins, and reliable sales-to-installation handoffs as volume increases.

| Fewer errors | Avoided redesigns, repeat surveys, and pricing mistakes |
| Less administration | Reduced duplicate entry between proposals, contracts, and CRM |

These are plausible benefits, not guaranteed outcomes. For example, Aurora publishes customer reports of faster proposals and fewer change orders, but these are vendor-selected case studies—not forecasts for your business. Aurora customer examples

2. Calculate ROI against your current workflow

ROI = (incremental benefits − incremental costs) ÷ incremental costs × 100

Use the same period for both, typically one year.

Benefits can include:

Labour value: proposals × hours saved per proposal × fully loaded hourly cost.

Additional contribution profit: extra completed installations × profit per installation after variable costs.

Avoided costs: fewer errors, outsourced designs, or unnecessary visits.

Costs should include subscriptions, usage charges, onboarding, training time, integrations, and migration—minus any existing expenses you eliminate.

Important: Saved employee time is capacity, not automatically cash savings. Count its financial value only if it reduces spending or gets productively redeployed. Don’t count the same time twice as both labour savings and extra sales.

3. Illustrative example

These are assumptions, not industry benchmarks; all amounts use the same currency.

| Monthly input | Amount |
|---|---:|
| Proposals produced | 80 |
| Time saved per proposal | 30 minutes |
| Loaded labour cost | $40/hour |
| Value of capacity freed | $1,600 |
| Recurring software cost | $600 |

If you fully realize that labour value:

Monthly net benefit: $1,000.

Recurring-cost ROI: 167%, before setup costs.

Labour-only break-even: 30 proposals per month.

If the time remains unused and payroll stays unchanged, the cash return could instead be negative. Additional profitable installations could change that—but should be measured, not assumed.

4. Compare against a realistic alternative

The baseline shouldn’t necessarily be manual spreadsheets. OpenSolar offers its core design, sales, and management platform free, with paid enterprise services. That means a paid product must justify its incremental value over a suitable free option, including differences in training, accuracy, and workflow fit. OpenSolar services and pricing

5. Validate before committing

Run a pilot using comparable leads and track:

Total staff time per proposal, including revisions.

Proposal turnaround time.

Completed-install conversion and cancellations.

Contribution profit and rework costs.

Start with zero assumed conversion improvement in your conservative case, then update it when enough installations have completed.

Are you evaluating a particular platform, and roughly how many proposals does your team produce per month?

snapshots.query: what is automated solar proposal software
snapshots.answerText:
Automated solar proposal software helps solar installers and sales teams create customer-ready quotes without manually assembling designs, calculations, and sales documents.

Depending on the platform, it can:

Design a solar system: use an address and roof imagery to suggest panel placement.

Estimate electricity generation: account for sunlight and shading.

Calculate pricing and projected savings: present system costs and financing options.

Generate a branded proposal: combine the design and estimates into a digital presentation or PDF.

Help close the sale: offer contracts and electronic signatures. Aurora Solar, proposal documentation

In plain English: you enter the customer’s property and energy-use information, and the software does much of the work needed to show them what solar could look like and cost.

Examples include Aurora Solar and OpenSolar, which combine design automation with customer proposals. Aurora Solar, OpenSolar

“Automated” doesn’t mean guaranteed—generation and savings are estimates, and the installer still needs to verify the inputs and installation feasibility.

snapshots.query: why is accurate solar system design crucial for proposals
snapshots.answerText:
Accurate solar system design is crucial because a proposal’s price, energy forecast, and savings estimates all depend on it.

Realistic production: Accounting for shading, panel orientation, system size, and losses helps avoid overstating electricity generation. PVWatts design guidance

Credible savings: Production must be matched with the customer’s electricity use, utility rates, and export compensation to estimate savings realistically. DOE homeowner’s guide

A buildable, properly scoped system: Selecting suitable mounting, inverters, and any batteries helps ensure the proposal covers more than just panels. DOE design basics

Fewer surprises: In practical terms, getting these details right reduces the risk of redesigns, unexpected costs, and disappointed customers.

Bottom line: Accurate design makes a proposal a credible delivery plan—not just a sales pitch.
